title: Voting systems
examples: What is the difference between first past the post and proportional representation?
When would a country use a preferential voting system?
Which voting system gives every vote more weight?

explain.say: Today we are learning about different ways to count votes.
First we look at first past the post voting, or FPTP.
In FPTP, the candidate with the most votes wins the seat.
Next is proportional representation, or PR.
Finally, we have preferential voting, which asks for rankings.
Consider a local election for a single council seat.

items: Preferential | Candidate with most first choices

faq.q: Does FPTP mean everyone votes for the same person?
faq.a: No, it does not mean that. It only means that the candidate with the highest number of votes wins the single seat.
asks: What is the main rule of FPTP?

faq.q: How is proportional representation different from FPTP?
faq.a: PR tries to make the seats won match the percentage of votes a party received overall. FPTP does not guarantee this match.
asks: Does PR give everyone a fair chance?
Is PR always used in large countries?

faq.q: What exactly do I do when I vote preferentially?
faq.a: You rank candidates in order of preference, like first, second, and third. If your first choice fails, your vote moves to your second choice.
asks: How does preferential voting work step-by-step?
Do I have to rank every single person?

faq.q: Are these voting systems used everywhere in the world?
faq.a: No, different countries use different systems based on their history and political goals. For example, some countries use PR more often.
asks: Is one system better than the others?
Does the country decide the system?

faq.q: If I vote for a small party, what happens with FPTP?
faq.a: In FPTP, your vote for a small party might not help that party win a seat, even if many people vote for them.
asks: What is the main weakness of FPTP?

facts: FPTP awards a seat to the candidate with the most votes in a single area.
Proportional representation aims for the seats won to reflect the votes received.
Preferential voting allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference.
These systems determine how votes translate into elected seats.

quiz.say: A country has three parties with 50%, 30%, and 20% of the vote. Under FPTP, how many seats would the parties likely get if there are three seats available?

options.show: All three parties would get one seat.
options.say: All three parties would get one seat.

options.show: The party with 30% would win all three seats.
options.say: The party with 30% would win all three seats.

options.show: The party with 50% of the vote would win at least one seat.
options.say: The party with 50% of the vote would win at least one seat.

quiz.why: FPTP means the leading candidate takes the seat, so the 50% party is most likely to win the first seat.

wrong.0: This is wrong because FPTP only awards seats based on winning local contests, not total votes.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the party with the highest percentage of votes is usually the most likely winner.
wrong.3: This is wrong because FPTP does not divide seats by vote percentage.

quiz.say: If a voter ranks Candidate A as first, Candidate B as second, and Candidate C as third, which system is this vote designed for?
quiz.why: Preferential voting requires you to rank candidates in order of how much you prefer them.

wrong.0: This is wrong because PR focuses on the total percentage of votes, not the ranking order.
wrong.1: This is wrong because a simple majority only counts the highest single vote count.
wrong.3: This is wrong because FPTP only counts the first preference vote.

quiz.say: Which system aims to make the number of seats a party wins closely match the percentage of votes they received?
quiz.why: Proportional representation is specifically designed to ensure fairness in seat allocation based on vote share.

wrong.1: This is wrong because FPTP can lead to a mismatch between votes and seats.
wrong.2: This is wrong because preferential voting is about voter preference order, not overall proportionality.
wrong.3: This is wrong because a simple majority only guarantees a win in one area, not overall proportionality.
